summary: The Netherlands is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, nationals of the countries on the EU's visa-exempt list can stay 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorization is not yet in operation), and everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa costing €90.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: the Schengen Borders Code counts the 180-day period preceding each day of stay, so days already spent anywhere in the area during that period still count against the 90. The day you enter counts as the first day of stay and the day you leave as the last.

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and/or photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders, and passports are no longer stamped. Registration happens at the border on your first crossing since the EES started; the EU says it can be quicker if you register some data in advance at a self-service kiosk or through a mobile app, where available. The UK government's travel advice says there is no cost for EES registration.

notes: Entering from outside the EU, the duty-free allowance is 200 cigarettes (or 100 cigarillos, 50 cigars or 250 g of tobacco), 1 litre of spirits over 22% (or 2 litres of fortified or sparkling wine), 4 litres of still wine, 16 litres of beer, and other goods worth up to €300 (€430 by air or sea), according to the EU’s Your Europe portal.

Arriving from another EU country, you pay no duty on alcohol and tobacco bought for your own use; above guideline levels (such as 800 cigarettes or 10 litres of spirits) customs may ask you to show they are for personal use.

tips.text: The 90-day limit counts across the entire Schengen Area, not just the Netherlands — days spent in Belgium or Germany count against the same allowance.

Cyclists have priority over other traffic (Government of Canada), and the UK FCDO warns that cycle paths are busy and cyclists ride at speed. On foot, make sure you are not walking on a bike path — they often run alongside pavements and are not always clearly marked — and look out for bikes and trams when crossing.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for the Netherlands?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit the Netherlands and the rest of the Schengen Area visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period. Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, they will need to obtain this online authorization (€20) before travel.

faq.question: How much does a Netherlands Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged 6–11. It allows stays of up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen countries.

faq.question: How do I stay in the Netherlands longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: You need a residence permit from the IND (Immigration and Naturalisation Service). Its fee table lists €254 for family, study and most other purposes and €423 for paid employment, highly skilled migrants and self-employment.

faq.question: What is the Dutch orientation year (zoekjaar) permit?
faq.answer: It is a residence permit to look for work in the Netherlands after study, a doctorate or scientific research. The IND fee is €254. No official source we could read states the eligibility conditions.

faq.question: Is cash widely accepted in the Netherlands?
faq.answer: The Government of Canada says credit cards are not widely accepted in the Netherlands and advises making sure you have access to enough cash to cover your expenses during your trip.
